icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saints Constantine and Helen flanking the True Cross, both crowned and robed in royal red and gold, with Greek inscriptions above their heads

saints.life_story:
Constantine was the Roman emperor in the years just after Christianity stopped being illegal. For three hundred years before him, being a Christian could get you killed by the Roman state. Constantine changed that. In the year 313 he signed an edict that gave Christians freedom to worship openly. Twelve years later, in 325, he called the great gathering of bishops at Nicaea that gave the Church the Creed Orthodox Christians still say every Sunday.

Helen was his mother. She became a Christian later in life and turned out to be one of the most determined pilgrims the Church has ever known. When she was already in her seventies, she made the long journey from Constantinople to Jerusalem and walked the holy places herself, asking the local Christians to show her where Christ had lived and died. She found the place of the crucifixion, had it excavated, and uncovered the True Cross — the actual cross Jesus had been nailed to. Constantine built churches there, at her direction, that still stand.

The Church calls them both Equal-to-the-Apostles. The apostles preached Christ; Constantine and Helen gave Christ's Church a place to stand in the world. They are commemorated together on May 21.

callouts.title: THE GOLD HALOS
callouts.body: Look at the gold circles around both their heads. That's how an icon says they are holy. Every saint has one — it's the first thing to look for. The gold isn't paint pretending to be light; it's the icon telling you the light of God is in them.

callouts.title: THE TRUE CROSS BETWEEN THEM
callouts.body: Between Constantine and Helen the icon almost always shows a tall cross. That's the True Cross — the one Helen found in Jerusalem. The icon is saying: she went looking, she found it, and the cross still stands between them. It's the reason they share a feast day.

callouts.title: ROYAL RED AND GOLD
callouts.body: Their robes are royal red and gold. Real Roman emperors and empresses wore this kind of color — but the icon dresses them this way for a deeper reason too. They were a king and queen on earth, but the icon is naming them king and queen of a much bigger kingdom. The colors say: they belong to it now.

alternate_names: Mary the Myrrhbearer & wife of Cleopas
Mary the Myrrhbearer and wife of Cleopas

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saint Mary the Myrrhbearer holding a small alabaster jar of myrrh, haloed, wearing a deep red maphorion over a darker tunic

saints.life_story:
Mary lived in Jerusalem in the last days of Christ's life. She was the wife of Cleopas — the same Cleopas who, with another disciple, would meet the risen Christ on the road to Emmaus and not recognize him until he broke bread with them. The Gospel of John names her as a kinswoman of the Mother of God.

She stood at the cross. When most of the men ran, she did not. Before dawn on the third day she went with the other myrrhbearing women to the tomb, carrying spices to anoint Christ's body. They did not yet know he had risen. They asked each other as they walked, "Who will roll away the stone for us?" The stone was already moved when they arrived. An angel told them what no one else yet knew: "He is not here. He is risen."

The Church remembers Mary the Myrrhbearer because she stood when most fled, and she brought what she had to where Christ lay. The women carrying the spices were the first to be told the news that changed the world.

callouts.title: THE HANDS HOLDING MYRRH
callouts.body: See how she holds the small jar with both hands at the level of her heart. That's not just a way to carry it. In icons, hands always say something. Hers say: she brought what she had — burial spices for the body of a friend — and she walked to the place of death to give them.

callouts.title: THE ALABASTER JAR
callouts.body: The little vessel she holds is the alabaster jar of myrrh — the perfumed oil her people used to anoint the dead. Saints often hold the thing that tells you who they are. Mary holds the jar she carried to the tomb. The icon names her by what she brought.

callouts.title: THE RED VEIL
callouts.body: Her head is wrapped in a deep red veil — the maphorion. The Mother of God wears one too, usually larger and reaching her shoulders. In icons, women who walked with Christ wear this veil. It says she belongs to the people who stood beneath the cross.

saints.display_name: The Holy Fathers of the First Council
alternate_names: Holy Fathers of the First Ecumenical Council
Holy Fathers of the 1st Ecumenical Council

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of the Holy Fathers of the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, bishops seated in tiers holding a long scroll of the Creed between them, the heretic Arius cast down at the foot of the composition

saints.life_story:
In the year 325, three hundred and eighteen bishops came from all across the Christian world and gathered in a Roman city called Nicaea. The emperor Constantine — the same Constantine the Church commemorates on May 21 — had called them. The Church had a problem to settle. A priest named Arius was teaching that Christ was not truly God but only the highest of God's creatures. If Arius was right, the Christian faith would no longer be Christian.

The bishops came from Egypt, Syria, Greece, Italy, the lands of the Goths, and even further east. Among them was Athanasius, then a young deacon helping his bishop, who would spend the next fifty years of his life defending what was decided at Nicaea. Spyridon of Trimythous came from Cyprus — a shepherd-bishop who held up a brick to show how the Trinity could be three and one. Nicholas of Myra was there — the bishop whose name children still know.

Together the bishops wrote down what the Church had always believed: that Christ is God "of one essence with the Father, begotten not made." We call what they wrote the Creed. Orthodox Christians still stand and say it every Sunday.

callouts.title: THE SCROLL THEY HOLD
callouts.body: In most icons of this feast, the bishops are shown together holding a single long scroll between them. The scroll is the Creed — the words they wrote at Nicaea. Saints often hold the thing that names them. These bishops are named by the words the Church says every Sunday because of them.

callouts.title: THE BISHOP'S BAND
callouts.body: Look at the long bands of cloth running over their shoulders, marked with black crosses. That's the omophorion — what bishops wear in icons and still wear at the altar today. The crosses on it say: this is the shepherd who carries the cross of Christ for the people in his care.

callouts.title: A WHOLE ROW OF HALOS
callouts.body: Look at the row of gold halos. Three hundred and eighteen bishops came to Nicaea; not all of them are shown, but the ones in the icon all have halos. The icon is saying these are not just men who met in a city. The Church is naming all of them holy.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saint John the Forerunner in the wilderness, gaunt and bearded, wearing a camel-hair tunic under a green-brown mantle, haloed, holding a small scroll with the words 'Behold the Lamb of God'

saints.life_story:
John was the cousin of Christ. His mother Elizabeth and the Mother of God were kin. He was born to elderly parents who had given up hope of having children, and he grew up in the wilderness, in the rough country east of Jerusalem.

The Gospels remember what he wore: a tunic of camel's hair tied with a leather belt around his waist. He ate locusts and wild honey. He came out of the wilderness preaching repentance and baptizing people in the Jordan river. When Christ came to him to be baptized, the Father spoke from heaven and the Spirit descended on Christ as a dove. John was the last and greatest of the prophets — the voice in the wilderness sent ahead of Christ to make the way ready.

He pointed to Christ and said, "Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world." He was imprisoned by King Herod for telling the king he could not marry his brother's wife, and he was beheaded in prison. The Church calls him the Forerunner — the one who ran ahead.

Today the Church remembers a specific moment in her history: the third time the Forerunner's relics were found and returned to the faithful, after being hidden for safekeeping in dangerous times.

callouts.title: CAMEL-HAIR AND WILDERNESS GREEN
callouts.body: In every icon John wears the same distinctive clothing: a rough tunic of camel hair under a deeper outer mantle, often a dark green or olive. No other saint is dressed this way. The icon is saying who he is by what he wore — the prophet from the wilderness, not from any city or palace.

callouts.title: THE PROPHET'S GAZE
callouts.body: His face is gaunt, his eyes deep-set, his hair wild. He looks out at you with the gaze of someone who has spent his life in the wilderness watching for the Lord. The icon does not soften him. It shows him the way he was — a voice crying in the desert.

callouts.title: THE SCROLL HE HOLDS
callouts.body: Often in his icon, John holds a small scroll with words written on it: "Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world." That was the thing he said when he saw Christ. The icon is naming him by what he said. His scroll is his life's one sentence.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of the Venerable Bede in a monk's black robe, haloed, seated or standing with an open Gospel book in his hands, a quill at his side

saints.life_story:
Bede was an English monk who lived from 672 to 735. He was sent to a monastery in northern England when he was seven years old and never left it. He spent the rest of his life there — almost sixty years — praying, copying manuscripts, and writing.

He wrote a book called the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the great history of how Christianity came to the people of England. Without his writing, we would have lost most of what we know about the early English Christians. The Church has called him "Venerable" for thirteen hundred years — a title given to almost no other saint.

On the last morning of his life he was dictating a translation of the Gospel of John, sentence by sentence, to a young monk who was writing it down. The boy said, "There is only one chapter left, but it is hard for you to speak." Bede answered, "Write quickly." When the boy said the work was finished, Bede said, "It is finished," and he died.

Bede lived three hundred years before the Christian Church of the East and the Church of the West were divided. The Orthodox Church still honors him on May 27 — one of her saints, the same as any other.

callouts.title: THE LETTERS ABOVE HIS HEAD
callouts.body: Look at the letters above his head. In Orthodox icons the Church writes saint names in Greek — even an English saint like Bede. The pattern is the same: Ο ΑΓΙΟΣ for a man, Η ΑΓΙΑ for a woman, meaning "the holy one," then the saint's name. The Church names her saints in the language she first prayed in.

callouts.title: THE BOOK IN HIS HANDS
callouts.body: Bede is almost always shown holding a book — the Gospels he loved and translated, or his own history of the English Church. Saints often hold what they made or what they kept. He was a writer his whole life. The icon hands him back the book that was always in his hands.

callouts.title: A MONK'S BLACK ROBE
callouts.body: He wears the black robe of a monk. In icons, black says the world is dead to him — he has given his life entirely to prayer. Bede entered the monastery at seven and never left. The robe is the visible sign of a life that belonged to one place and one God.

saints.display_name: Saints Macrina the Elder and Emilia
alternate_names: Macrina, grandmother of St. Basil the Great
Emilia, mother of Saint Basil the Great

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saints Macrina the Elder and Emilia, two haloed women side by side, both in dark robes and head-veils, faces frontal, Greek inscriptions naming each saint above her head

saints.life_story:
Macrina was the grandmother of St. Basil the Great. She lived in Cappadocia during the worst years of the Roman persecutions, and as a young woman she fled with her husband into the forests and lived hidden there for seven years. When the persecutions ended, she came back and taught her family the faith she had carried into the wilderness.

Emilia was her granddaughter-in-law, the wife of Macrina's grown son. Emilia raised ten children with him in the same household in Caesarea. Of those ten, five became saints. Her oldest son Basil became one of the greatest bishops the Church has ever known. Her daughter Macrina the Younger followed her grandmother's name into a life of prayer. Two more of her sons, Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste, became bishops.

The Church remembers these two women on the same day because the holiness of one became the foundation of the holiness of the next. The grandmother who hid in the forest taught the mother. The mother bore the saints. Both names belong together at the root of a family the Church will never stop thanking God for.

callouts.title: THE FACES THAT LOOK OUT
callouts.body: Both women face forward, eyes open, looking out at whoever holds the icon. Icons almost always do this. It is the way the Church says: these saints are not somewhere far away or long ago — they are alive in Christ now, and the icon is the window where you can meet them. Macrina and Emilia are looking back.

callouts.title: THEIR NAMES IN GREEK
callouts.body: Above each head, written in Greek: Η ΑΓΙΑ ΜΑΚΡΙΝΑ over the grandmother, Η ΑΓΙΑ ΕΜΜΕΛΕΙΑ over Emilia. The Η ΑΓΙΑ means "the holy one" — feminine. The same form as the Ο ΑΓΙΟΣ that names a male saint, but the ending changes. The Church writes their names the way she speaks of them in her prayers.

callouts.title: THE DARK ROBES OF MOTHERS
callouts.body: Both women wear deep dark robes and head-veils. Macrina the elder lived as a wife and grandmother, hidden in the forest in dangerous years; Emilia raised her children at home. Yet both are shown wearing the deep dark colors more often seen on monastics. The icon is saying that their lives, however lived, belonged wholly to God.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of the Holy Pentecost: the twelve apostles seated in a horseshoe composition, each with a small tongue of fire above his halo, the figure of Cosmos crowned and aged in the lower arch holding scrolls representing the nations

saints.life_story:
Fifty days after Pascha, the apostles were together in a room in Jerusalem. Christ had told them to wait. Suddenly a sound like a great wind filled the house, and what looked like tongues of fire came down and rested on each of them. They were filled with the Holy Spirit.

When they went out into the streets, every person there — and Jerusalem was full of people from every nation that had come for the feast — heard them speaking in his own language. Some of the crowd thought the apostles were drunk. Peter stood up and explained: the Spirit promised by the prophets had come, and the kingdom of God was beginning.

That day three thousand people were baptized.

The Church calls Pentecost her own birthday. Before that morning, the disciples were a frightened group hiding behind locked doors. After it, they were the Church — sent out, speaking, healing, gathering people from every nation into one body. The Holy Spirit who descended on them is the same Spirit who is poured out on every Christian at chrismation. He does not stop coming.

callouts.title: THE BOOKS THEY HOLD
callouts.body: In the icon, the apostles sit in a half-circle, and almost all of them hold a small book or a scroll. The books are the Gospels they will go preach. The scrolls are the prophecies come true. The icon is saying: the Spirit did not leave them empty-handed. He sent them out with the Word.

callouts.title: TWELVE HALOS, ONE FIRE
callouts.body: Look at the row of haloed heads. Each apostle has his own circle of gold; above each one, a small tongue of fire. The icon is saying the Spirit does not give one big light to all of them at once — he gives a tongue of fire to each, by name. The Church remembers them one by one.

callouts.title: FACES TURNED TO THE FIRE
callouts.body: Some apostles look up toward the fire; others look out toward you. The icon shows both at once. It is the moment the Spirit came down — and it is also the apostles, ever-since-then, looking out from the icon and waiting. Pentecost is both an event in time and a thing the Church still lives inside.

saints.display_name: Saint Justin the Philosopher and Martyr
alternate_names: Justin the Philosopher and Martyr and his Companions

icon.source: TBD — pending Kevin sourcing per D5 §5.1

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saint Justin the Philosopher, bearded and haloed, wearing the heavy outer mantle of a Greek philosopher, holding an open scroll in one hand and gesturing with the other

saints.life_story:
Justin grew up in a Roman city in Palestine, the son of pagan parents. He spent his youth studying philosophy — first the Stoics, then the Pythagoreans, then Aristotle, then Plato. He was looking for the truth.

One day, walking on the seashore, he met an old man. They talked. The old man pointed Justin to the Hebrew prophets, who he said had spoken of the truth long before any Greek philosopher had. Justin read them and became a Christian. But he did not stop being a philosopher — he kept wearing the philosopher's cloak, and he started writing in defense of the Christians.

He wrote two long letters to the Roman emperors, asking them to stop killing Christians. He explained that what Christians believed was reasonable, that the truth Plato had reached for was Christ all along. He called this the "seeds of the Word" — scattered through every culture and every wise person, waiting to be recognized.

Under the emperor Marcus Aurelius, Justin was arrested in Rome with six companions and brought before the prefect Rusticus. Asked if he believed that he would be rewarded in heaven for being a Christian, he answered that he did not just believe — he knew. He was beheaded that same day.

callouts.title: THE PHILOSOPHER'S SCROLL
callouts.body: Justin holds a scroll — the sign of a teacher who wrote things down. Saints who were theologians or philosophers almost always hold a scroll in their icon, not a Gospel book. The icon is saying he is named by what he wrote. His books defended the Christians at the cost of his life.

callouts.title: THE PHILOSOPHER'S MANTLE
callouts.body: He wears a heavy outer mantle — the tribon, the cloak Greek philosophers wore. Justin kept wearing it after becoming a Christian. The icon shows him in it on purpose. He was a philosopher who became a Christian and stayed a philosopher. Whatever in philosophy was true, he said, was already from Christ.

callouts.title: A HAND THAT POINTS
callouts.body: One hand holds the scroll; the other is raised, palm open, fingers pointing slightly. In icons of teachers and writers, hands say something different from a bishop's blessing. This is the hand of someone explaining. The icon is showing him in the middle of making his argument.

quoted_attribution.speaker: St. Justin the Philosopher
quoted_attribution.text: I do not suppose; I know and am fully persuaded.
quoted_attribution.source: answering the prefect Rusticus at his trial in Rome, c. 165 AD

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saint Kevin of Glendalough in a black monastic robe, haloed, one hand open at his side with a small blackbird resting in his palm, the other holding a crozier or a small model of his monastic church

saints.life_story:
Kevin was born in Ireland around the year 498 and grew up at a time when the Christian faith had only recently come to his island. As a young man he went into the mountains of Wicklow, in the eastern part of Ireland, and made his home in a tiny stone cave in the cliff above a lake. He lived there alone, praying.

One of the most loved stories about him is the story of the blackbird. He was praying with his arm held out the way the monks of his land prayed, and a blackbird flew down and laid an egg in his open palm. He did not move. He held his arm still for as long as it took the bird to hatch the egg and fly away.

Other Christians began to find him in his cave. Over the years, a monastery grew around the place. Glendalough — the glen of two lakes — became one of the great centers of learning in early Ireland. Monks copied books there, and young men were trained there to be sent out as missionaries.

Kevin lived a very long life and never left the glen. The Orthodox Church received him as one of her saints — Celtic and Eastern Christian alike — because he lived before the Church of the East and the Church of the West were divided.

callouts.title: THE MONK'S BLACK ROBE
callouts.body: Kevin wears the long black robe of a monastic — the same kind of robe a monk wears today. In icons, black says the world is dead to him; he lives only for prayer. Kevin spent his whole adult life in one mountain glen, so the robe fits him. The icon is showing a man who chose stillness.

callouts.title: THE OPEN HAND
callouts.body: Often Kevin is shown with one hand open, palm up — the gesture of a monk in prayer in the Irish tradition. The same icon-makers who knew the blackbird story painted his hand wide and still. In icons, hands are never accidental. His says: he held it open long enough for something else to make a home there.

callouts.title: A SMALL CHURCH IN HIS ARM
callouts.body: In some icons Kevin cradles a small church building under one arm. That's how the iconographers say he founded a monastery — they hand him back the place he made. Other icons give him a crozier, the staff of an abbot. Either way, the icon is naming him by what he built.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saints Mary and Martha of Bethany, two haloed women side by side, Mary in deep red and holding a small alabaster jar, Martha in olive-green and carrying a serving cloth or vessel

saints.life_story:
Mary and Martha were sisters who lived in Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem. Their brother was Lazarus. Christ came to their house often. They were among the few people who fed him and gave him a place to rest during the years he was traveling.

The Gospel of Luke tells the story of an evening when Christ came to visit. Martha was busy with the work of welcoming him — cooking, serving, making the house ready. Mary sat down at his feet and listened to him talk. Martha came in and asked Christ to send Mary to help her. Christ answered gently: "Mary has chosen the better part, and it will not be taken from her."

Later, when their brother Lazarus died, it was Martha who ran out to meet Christ on the road. "If you had been here, my brother would not have died," she said. Christ raised Lazarus from the tomb four days later.

A few days after that, at a dinner in their home, Mary took a jar of very costly perfume and poured it over Christ's feet, drying them with her hair. The smell of it filled the whole house. Some of the disciples objected. Christ defended her: she had done it, he said, for his burial.

callouts.title: TWO SISTERS LOOKING OUT
callouts.body: Both sisters face forward, eyes open, side by side. Icons of paired women friends keep them close this way. They look out at you not as figures from a long-ago Gospel story but as women still in the room where Christ used to come. The icon does not move them into the past.

callouts.title: WHAT EACH ONE HOLDS
callouts.body: Look at what each sister holds. Mary almost always carries a small jar — the same alabaster jar Mary the Myrrhbearer carries, but a different Mary and a different jar. This one is the perfume she poured at Christ's feet. Martha sometimes holds a cloth or a small bowl — the things of welcome, of serving the guest.

callouts.title: THE COLORS OF SISTERS
callouts.body: Their robes are dark and rich — Mary often in a deep red, Martha in a green-brown or olive. The icons show them as they were: women of a household, not nuns and not queens. They belonged to a quiet life that Christ chose to enter again and again.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of the Sunday of All Saints: Christ enthroned at the top, the Mother of God and John the Forerunner near him, beneath them tiers of apostles, bishops, martyrs, monastics, kings, queens, holy children, and unnamed faithful, every figure haloed and turned toward Christ

saints.life_story:
The Sunday after Pentecost the Church does not commemorate a single saint or a single feast. She commemorates all of them. Every saint, named and unnamed, known and unknown, who has ever lived and died in Christ. They are too many to list in a calendar of three hundred and sixty-five days. So one Sunday holds them all.

The icon of this feast is one of the most crowded in the Orthodox tradition. Christ is enthroned at the top. The Mother of God and John the Forerunner stand near him. Beneath them, the apostles in a row. Beneath them, the bishops and martyrs and monks and nuns. Beneath them, the holy kings and queens, the wonderworkers, the children, the missionaries. At the very bottom, ordinary Christians — the saints whose names no calendar has — turn their faces up toward Christ.

The Church places this feast right after Pentecost on purpose. The Holy Spirit came down at Pentecost and made the Church; now the Church shows what the Spirit has done with two thousand years. Every face in the icon is the Spirit's work. The feast is also the Church's confession that she does not yet know all her saints — some of them are alive now, walking around, and will be added to the icon long after this Sunday is forgotten.

callouts.title: A CROWD OF HALOS
callouts.body: Look at how many gold halos are in this one icon. Dozens of them, sometimes hundreds. Each circle is the Church saying: this one too is holy. The icon teaches by repetition. What a halo means is the same on every head. The communion of saints is not an idea — it is a crowd.

callouts.title: EVERY KIND OF ROBE
callouts.body: In one icon you can see almost every kind of clothing the Church remembers. Bishops in omophorion. Monks in black. Martyrs in red. Kings and queens in royal purple. Holy children in white. The icon is showing that holiness has no single uniform. Every life given to Christ becomes itself an icon.

callouts.title: ALL FACES LOOK UP
callouts.body: Notice that almost every face in the lower rows is turned up toward Christ. The saints are not facing the viewer here — they are facing him. The icon is teaching the direction holiness flows. They became saints because they spent their lives looking that way.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saint Cyril of Alexandria, haloed and bearded, in bishop's vestments with white omophorion bearing black crosses, holding a Gospel book in one hand and raising the other in blessing

saints.life_story:
Cyril was the bishop of Alexandria in Egypt — patriarch of the great Christian city on the Nile delta — from the year 412 until he died in 444. Alexandria in those years was one of the four most important Christian cities in the world.

The crisis of Cyril's life was a fight over a title. A bishop in Constantinople named Nestorius had said that Mary should not be called the Mother of God, but only the mother of Christ — as if Christ-the-man and Christ-the-God were two different persons living in one body. Cyril answered him over many years and many letters: Christ is not two persons but one. The eternal Word of God was born of Mary as a baby. So the baby in her arms is true God. So she is rightly called the Mother of God.

The Church gathered for a great council at Ephesus in 431 to settle the question. Cyril's writing carried the day. The Council confirmed what most Christians had already always sung in their prayers: Mary is the Theotokos, the God-bearer.

Cyril is sometimes called the Pillar of Faith. Without him, the Church might have lost the language of who Christ is — one Person, fully God and fully man — and the Mother of God might have been called by a smaller name.

callouts.title: THE BISHOP'S LONG BAND
callouts.body: Cyril wears the omophorion — the long white band running over his shoulders, marked with black crosses. Every Orthodox bishop, then and now, wears it. The crosses on it say: this is the man who carries the cross of Christ for the people in his care. The omophorion is the most recognizable sign of a bishop in any icon.

callouts.title: THE GOSPEL HE GUARDED
callouts.body: Cyril holds a Gospel book bound in gold. Bishops in icons almost always hold one. The Gospel is what they preached, what they defended, what they died for. Cyril's life was a long defense of what is on the very first page of that book: that the Word was made flesh.

callouts.title: THE BLESSING HAND
callouts.body: His other hand is raised in blessing — three fingers together, two fingers folded down. Three for the Holy Trinity, two for Christ's two natures. The same hand sign Christ makes in icons, and every Orthodox priest still makes when he blesses people. Cyril's blessing hand is also his theology: God is three, Christ is one.

quoted_attribution.speaker: St. Cyril of Alexandria
quoted_attribution.text: The holy Virgin is rightly called the Mother of God.
quoted_attribution.source: Third Letter to Nestorius, 430 AD — adopted by the Council of Ephesus, 431

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saints Bartholomew and Barnabas, two haloed apostles standing side by side, each holding a Gospel book, one with the other hand raised in blessing

saints.life_story:
The Church remembers two apostles on this day — one of the Twelve and one of the Seventy.

Bartholomew was one of the original twelve disciples Christ chose. The Gospel of John remembers him under another name: Nathanael, the man Christ first saw "under the fig tree." After Pentecost he went out, like the rest of the Twelve, to preach the resurrection. Tradition says he carried the Gospel as far as India and Armenia, and that he was killed for it there.

Barnabas was not one of the Twelve. He was an early Christian from the island of Cyprus, a Jew named Joseph whom the apostles renamed Barnabas — "son of encouragement." He sold a field he owned and laid the money at the apostles' feet. He brought the newly converted Paul to the other apostles when they were still afraid of him. He traveled with Paul as a missionary, and later went back to Cyprus and founded the Church there. He was killed in his own homeland.

The Church remembers them together on June 11. Cyprus claims Barnabas as her own founder. The Armenians claim Bartholomew. Two apostles, two distant homelands, one day. The Church's reach has always been wider than any one place.

callouts.title: APOSTOLIC HANDS
callouts.body: Look at their hands. Often one apostle is shown raising a hand in blessing — three fingers together for the Trinity, two folded for Christ's two natures. The other often holds a scroll or a Gospel in one hand while the other gestures outward, as if speaking. Apostles' hands in icons are always doing the work of preaching.

callouts.title: A GOSPEL EACH
callouts.body: Each apostle holds a Gospel book bound in gold or red leather. Apostles almost always carry one — they are the ones who first preached the Good News. Tradition says Barnabas was buried with a copy of Matthew's Gospel; centuries later, when his tomb was found in Cyprus, the book was still there.

callouts.title: TWO MEN FROM DIFFERENT LANDS
callouts.body: The two apostles stand side by side and look out from the icon together, but their faces are not the same. Bartholomew is often darker-bearded, in the style of the Holy Land. Barnabas is lighter, in the style of Cyprus. Icons let saints look like the people they came from. The Church does not erase where they were born.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saint Augustine of Hippo in bishop's vestments with white omophorion, haloed, bearded, holding a Gospel book in one hand, the other resting on a small flaming heart — the iconographic sign of his Confessions

saints.life_story:
Augustine was born in 354 in a small town in what is now Algeria, on the southern coast of the Mediterranean. His mother was a Christian — St. Monica, whom the Church remembers separately. His father was a pagan. Augustine grew up restless. He was brilliant, ambitious, and unhappy. For years he chased every philosophy and every pleasure he could find. His mother prayed for him.

When he was thirty-two, in the city of Milan, he heard Bishop Ambrose preaching. Something cracked in him. He sat in a garden weeping, and he heard a child somewhere singing a little song: "Take and read, take and read." He opened a Bible to where it fell and read a single verse from Paul. He was baptized that Easter.

He went back to North Africa. He became a bishop of a small port city called Hippo. He stayed there for the rest of his life — preaching, writing, defending the Church through theological storms. He wrote a book called the Confessions, the long story of how he found God, addressed to God himself. It is still one of the most-read books in the Christian world.

He died in the year 430 as the Vandals were laying siege to Hippo. The Orthodox Church commemorates him as one of her own — a Father of the pre-schism Christian West.

callouts.title: A WESTERN NAME IN GREEK
callouts.body: The letters above his head are Greek: Ο ΑΓΙΟΣ ΑΥΓΟΥΣΤΙΝΟΣ. The Greek-speaking Orthodox Church writes Augustine's name in her own language — even though Augustine spent his whole life writing in Latin. The Church names her saints in the language of her first prayers, no matter where they were from.

callouts.title: THE BISHOP'S OMOPHORION
callouts.body: He wears the long white band over his shoulders marked with crosses — the omophorion of an Orthodox bishop. In the West he is usually painted in different robes, but in the icons of the Eastern Church he wears what every bishop in her tradition wears. The Church receives him as her own bishop.

callouts.title: THE BOOK OF HIS HEART
callouts.body: In one hand he holds a Gospel book — the sign of a bishop. In some icons his other hand holds a small heart in flames, or rests on a small heart. That heart is his sign. The book he wrote about his own life — the Confessions — was the story of how his heart finally found its rest.

quoted_attribution.speaker: St. Augustine of Hippo
quoted_attribution.text: Our heart is restless until it rests in You.

icon.alt_text: Orthodox icon of Saint Jude the Apostle, haloed and bearded, in apostolic robes, holding a small scroll in one hand and gesturing outward with the other, his name written in Greek above his head

saints.life_story:
Jude, also called Thaddeus, was one of the twelve apostles Christ chose. He is not Judas Iscariot — the betrayer. He is a different man with a similar name, and the Church takes care to name him otherwise. Orthodox Christians often call him by his second name, Thaddeus, or by an older honor she gives him: Brother of the Lord. By tradition he was a son of Joseph the Betrothed from before Joseph was given charge of the Mother of God, and so he grew up in the household where Christ himself lived as a child.

After Pentecost, Jude went out to preach the resurrection. Tradition sends him into Mesopotamia, Armenia, and Persia — places the Church was first planted by foot and voice. There, sometime around the year sixty-five, he was killed for what he taught.

He wrote one short letter that the New Testament still keeps. In it he begs the Christians of his time to "contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints." The line still names what Orthodox Christians mean by Holy Tradition — the faith handed down once, and handed on still.

The Gospels remember his voice in one place. At the Last Supper he asked Christ a question — how God would reveal himself to those who loved him and not to the world. Christ's answer is part of the Gospel the Church reads on Jude's feast day.

callouts.title: THE SCROLL HE WROTE
callouts.body: Jude almost always holds a small scroll in his icon. The scroll is his epistle — the one letter he left the Church, only a single chapter long, but kept in the Bible for two thousand years. Saints often hold the thing that names them. Jude holds what he wrote.

callouts.title: HIS NAME IN GREEK
callouts.body: Above his head, in Greek: Ο ΑΓΙΟΣ ΙΟΥΔΑΣ Ο ΘΑΔΔΑΙΟΣ — "the holy Jude the Thaddeus." Icon-writers spell out both names on purpose. The Church writes saints' names the way she speaks them in her prayers, and for this Jude she takes care to say which Jude she means.

callouts.title: A PREACHER'S HAND
callouts.body: In his icon Jude often holds the scroll in one hand and gestures with the other — a hand open, palm slightly out, fingers reaching toward whoever is reading. Apostles in icons almost always do this. Their hands are the hands of preachers, caught in the middle of saying something. Jude's hand is still saying his one letter.
